cat > src/hooks/useSheet.ts <<'EOF'
import { useCallback, useEffect, useRef, useState } from "react";

/** Mirrors the CSS breakpoint below which the settings rail becomes a bottom sheet. */
export const SHEET_QUERY = "(max-width: 63.999rem)";

const FOCUSABLE =
  'a[href], button:not([disabled]), input:not([disabled]):not([type="hidden"]), select:not([disabled]), textarea:not([disabled]), [tabindex]:not([tabindex="-1"])';

/** Elements marked with this attribute become inert while the sheet is open. */
export const INERT_WHILE_SHEET = "data-inert-while-sheet";

function focusables(root: HTMLElement): HTMLElement[] {
  return [...root.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>(FOCUSABLE)].filter((el) => !el.closest("[hidden]"));
}

/**
 * Modal bottom sheet: focus moves in on open, Tab and Shift+Tab wrap inside it, the rest of the
 * page is inert, Escape closes, and focus returns to the button that opened it.
 */
export function useSheet(isSheet: boolean) {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
  const toggleRef = useRef<HTMLButtonElement>(null);
  const sheetRef = useRef<HTMLElement>(null);
  const active = open && isSheet;

  const close = useCallback(() => {
    setOpen(false);
    toggleRef.current?.focus();
  }, []);

  // Growing past the breakpoint turns the sheet back into the always-visible rail.
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!isSheet) setOpen(false);
  }, [isSheet]);

  useEffect(() => {
    const sheet = sheetRef.current;
    if (!active || !sheet) return;
    focusables(sheet)[0]?.focus();

    const outside = [...document.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>(`[${INERT_WHILE_SHEET}]`)];
    outside.forEach((el) => el.setAttribute("inert", ""));

    const onKey = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
      if (e.key === "Escape") {
        e.preventDefault();
        close();
        return;
      }
      if (e.key !== "Tab") return;
      const items = focusables(sheet);
      const first = items[0];
      const last = items[items.length - 1];
      if (!first || !last) return;
      const current = document.activeElement;
      if (e.shiftKey && (current === first || !sheet.contains(current))) {
        e.preventDefault();
        last.focus();
      } else if (!e.shiftKey && (current === last || !sheet.contains(current))) {
        e.preventDefault();
        first.focus();
      }
    };
    document.addEventListener("keydown", onKey);
    return () => {
      document.removeEventListener("keydown", onKey);
      outside.forEach((el) => el.removeAttribute("inert"));
    };
  }, [active, close]);

  return { open: active, setOpen, close, toggleRef, sheetRef };
}
EOF

import { afterEach, beforeEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from "vitest";
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";
import { ApiProvider } from "../api/ApiContext";
import { createMockClient } from "../api/client";
import { App } from "../App";
import { SHEET_QUERY } from "../hooks/useSheet";

function setViewport(mobile: boolean) {
  vi.stubGlobal("matchMedia", (query: string) => ({
    matches: query === SHEET_QUERY ? mobile : false,
    media: query,
    addEventListener: () => {},
    removeEventListener: () => {},
  }));
}

const renderApp = () =>
  render(
    <ApiProvider client={createMockClient(0)}>
      <App />
    </ApiProvider>,
  );

describe("settings sheet on a phone", () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    window.history.replaceState(null, "", "/");
    setViewport(true);

  it("is a named modal dialog that takes focus and makes the page inert", async () => {
    renderApp();

    expect(dialog).toHaveAttribute("aria-modal", "true");
    expect(dialog).toContainElement(document.activeElement as HTMLElement);
    expect(screen.getByRole("main", { hidden: true })).toHaveAttribute("inert");
    expect(opener.closest(".mobile-bar")).toHaveAttribute("inert");
  });

  it("wraps Tab and Shift+Tab inside the sheet", async () => {
    renderApp();
    await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Adjust" }));
    const done = screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Done" });
    const price = screen.getByRole("textbox", { name: /flat price/i });
    expect(done).toHaveFocus();

    price.focus();
    await userEvent.tab();
    expect(done).toHaveFocus();

    await userEvent.tab({ shift: true });
    expect(price).toHaveFocus();
  });

  it("returns focus to the opener and lifts inert on Escape and on Done", async () => {

    expect(screen.getByRole("main")).not.toHaveAttribute("inert");

    await userEvent.click(opener);
    await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: "Done" }));
    expect(opener).toHaveFocus();
  });

    setViewport(false);
    renderApp();
    expect(screen.queryByRole("dialog")).not.toBeInTheDocument();
    expect(screen.getByRole("complementary", { name: "Assumptions" })).toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});

def cheapest_by_tier(quotes: list[Quote]) -> dict[str, Quote | None]:
    result: dict[str, Quote | None] = {t: None for t in TIERS}
    for q in quotes:
        if not q.available:
            continue
        best = result.get(q.tier)
        if best is None or q.total < best.total:
            result[q.tier] = q
    return result


def cheapest_for_carrier(
    tables: RateTables, carrier: str, tier: str, parcel: Parcel, controls: Controls, year: int | None = None
) -> Quote | None:
@router.post("/quote", response_model=m.QuoteResponse)
def quote(body: m.QuoteRequest, tables: RateTables = Depends(get_tables)) -> dict:
    controls = to_controls(body.controls, tables, ["body", "controls"])
    quotes = quote_all(tables, to_parcel(body.parcel), controls)
    cheapest = cheapest_by_tier(quotes)
    return {
        "quotes": [quote_out(q) for q in quotes],
        "cheapest_by_tier": {
            tier: ({"carrier": q.carrier, "service_id": q.service_id, "total": float(q.total)} if q else None)
            for tier, q in cheapest.items()
        },
    }


@router.post("/breakeven", response_model=m.BreakevenResponse)
def breakeven(body: m.BreakevenRequest, tables: RateTables = Depends(get_tables)) -> dict:


def breakeven(
    tables: RateTables,
    controls: Controls,
    residential: bool,
    weights_lb: list[float] | None = None,
    distances_miles: list[float] | None = None,
) -> dict:
    weights = sorted(weights_lb) if weights_lb else default_weights(tables)
    distances = sorted(distances_miles) if distances_miles else default_distances(tables)
    carriers = [c for c in tables.carriers() if (c, controls.year) in tables.base_effective]

    cells = []
    bands = []
    for d in distances:
        first_loss: dict[str, float | None] = {c: None for c in PRIVATE}
        for w in weights:
            parcel = Parcel(weight_lb=w, distance_miles=d, residential=residential, speed=GROUND)
            quotes = {
                c: q
                for c in carriers
                if (q := cheapest_for_carrier(tables, c, GROUND, parcel, controls)) is not None
            }
            ranked = sorted(quotes.values(), key=lambda q: q.total)
            usps = quotes.get(USPS)
            for c in PRIVATE:
                other = quotes.get(c)
                if usps and other and first_loss[c] is None and usps.total >= other.total:
                    first_loss[c] = w
            private_zone = next((q.zone for q in ranked if q.carrier != USPS), None)
            cells.append(
                {
                    "weight_lb": w,
                    "distance_miles": d,
                    "zone_usps": zone_for(tables, USPS, d),
                    "zone_private": private_zone if private_zone is not None else zone_for(tables, "ups", d),
                    "winner": _pick(ranked[0]) if ranked else None,
                    "runner_up": _pick(ranked[1]) if len(ranked) > 1 else None,
                    "saving": float(ranked[1].total - ranked[0].total) if len(ranked) > 1 else 0.0,
                    "totals": {q.carrier: float(q.total) for q in ranked},
                }
            )
        bands.append(
            {
                "distance_miles": d,
                "zone_usps": zone_for(tables, USPS, d),
                "zone_private": zone_for(tables, "ups", d),
                "vs_ups": first_loss["ups"],
                "vs_fedex": first_loss["fedex"],
            }
        )
    return {
        "year": controls.year,
        "residential": residential,
        "weights_lb": weights,
        "distances_miles": distances,
        "cells": cells,
        "breakeven_weight_lb": bands,
    }

/** One entry of a 422 body, as backend/app/api/errors.py writes it: always loc, msg and type. */
export interface ValidationIssue {
  loc: (string | number)[];
  msg: string; // written for the shop owner; parcel-list errors start "Parcel N: "
  type: string; // the Pydantic error type, e.g. "less_than_equal"
}

/** 422 body. */
export interface ValidationErrorBody {
  detail: ValidationIssue[];
}

/** FastAPI's own errors (404, 405) carry a plain string; the client accepts both. */
export interface HttpErrorBody {
  detail: string;
}
''')

## PR #19 review fixes: all items done and pushed

Six commits, one per review item, pushed to `origin/issue-4-frontend-scaffold` (d119754 through 555530e, on top of your merge 8de9827). Tests (92 in 10 files), typecheck and build all pass. I did not touch `vite.config.ts` or `frontend/README.md`; the diff since 8de9827 is empty for both.

**HIGH 1, live responses checked (d119754).** Every response from the backend now goes through its endpoint's guard before the client returns it. If one has drifted, the client raises an `ApiError` saying the rate service answered POST /api/quote in an unexpected shape, giving the field path and what was expected. It also carries `contract.endpoint` and `contract.path` for code. Tests cover a renamed field (`total` became `price`) and a missing `limitations`. Cost: about 3 kB more gzipped in the main bundle.

**HIGH 2, decimal commas in CSVs (5a84f5d).** The parser now looks at Papa Parse's detected delimiter.
- **Semicolon file:** the comma is the decimal separator and `.` only groups thousands. `2,5` reads as 2.5 and `1.234,50` as 1234.5.
- **Comma file:** a quoted `"1,234"` reads as 1234. A quoted `"2,5"` reads as 2.5, because two digits after a comma can't be a thousands group.
- **Ambiguous values** (`1.234` in a semicolon file, `1,234` in a tab-delimited file) are never reinterpreted silently. Each gets a row warning naming the column and the reading used. That reading is the thousands one, and the warning says how to write the value unambiguously.
- I also replaced a literal invisible byte-order-mark character in the regex source with a `﻿` escape.

**MEDIUM 3, out-of-order loads (e0d3555).** `useParcelSet` now numbers each load. A load or error that finishes after a newer load, or after a clear, is dropped. The four new tests fail against the old hook and pass with the fix:
- a slow sample request resolving after a file upload;
- two sample requests resolving in reverse order;
- a superseded request that fails;
- a clear while a load is pending.

**MEDIUM 4, mobile settings sheet (12f828c).** The logic now lives in a `useSheet` hook, and `useMediaQuery` tracks the CSS breakpoint.
- **While open on a phone:** the sheet is `role="dialog"` with `aria-modal="true"`, named by its "Assumptions" heading. Focus moves to the sheet, and Tab and Shift+Tab wrap inside it.
- **Rest of the page:** made `inert`. The backdrop is no longer a focusable button.
- **Closing:** Escape or Done returns focus to Adjust. This happens only after `inert` is lifted, because an inert button can't take focus.
- **Wider screens:** past the breakpoint the sheet closes and becomes a plain labelled sidebar.

Tests cover the dialog name and focus, Tab wrapping, Escape and Done, and the desktop case. I also checked it in real Chromium at 375 px, since jsdom doesn't implement `inert`: Tab cycles Done → year → rate card → sliders → peak → price → Done, `main.inert` is true while open, and Escape puts focus back on Adjust.

**MEDIUM 5, fixed key sets in the guards (5b0f53d).** I checked the backend code and ran it for 2027:
- `cheapest_by_tier` always has all three tiers, with `null` when nothing can carry the parcel. The guard requires exactly those keys and the type is now `Record<Tier, …>`.
- Breakeven `totals` only lists carriers that publish the year and can carry the parcel. For 2027 that is `{"fedex": …}` with `runner_up: null`. The guard therefore allows only carrier keys but doesn't require all three.
- A cell's winner and runner-up must appear in its `totals`.
- `years`, `defaults.as_of` and `parcels_by_carrier` use the same carrier-keys-only check.

I added two real backend responses as fixtures, `breakeven-2027.json` and `quote-2027.json`, produced with FastAPI's `TestClient` against main after the PR #17 merge (5785f6f). The fixtures README now explains where they come from.

**LOW, `ValidationIssue.type` (555530e).** The backend's 422 entries are always exactly `{loc, msg, type}`, so `type` is now required, matching the guard. `ValidationErrorBody.detail` is the array only. FastAPI's own 404/405 errors, which send `detail` as a plain string, have a separate `HttpErrorBody` type, and the client still handles both.

```
"""Generate backend/app/sample_parcels.csv, the bundled ILLUSTRATIVE parcel mix.

This is an example, not real shipping data. It imitates a small online
home-goods shop (candles, mugs, linens, small decor): mostly light ground
parcels in small boxes, a minority of bulky boxes, and few expedited orders.

Target mix (issue #22):

- about 80 % of parcels weigh under 5 lb; every box except the bulky ones is
  under 1 cubic foot (1,728 cu in), so dimensional weight rarely applies;
- a fixed 12 rows of bulky boxes between 1 and 2 cubic feet (throws, lamps),
  about 7 % of parcels;
- a fixed 12 rows ship two to three day and 3 rows next day (about 4 % and
  1 % of parcels), always single light parcels; the rest ship ground;
- about 76 % of rows residential; distances spread over every zone, weighted
  toward the middle zones (3 to 6); five rows in delivery areas (four
  delivery area, one extended); two rows with non-standard packaging;
- 200 rows whose quantities sum to about 300 parcels.

Price charged. Ground parcels leave ``price_charged`` empty and use the flat
price control ($9.99 by default). Expedited parcels carry what a shop would
charge at checkout for faster shipping: $19.99 for two to three day and
$39.99 for next day. Small shops usually price an expedited option at two to
four times their standard rate, and these amounts sit near the published USPS
Priority Mail and Priority Mail Express prices for the light parcels people
choose to rush. Without them every expedited parcel would ship at $9.99 and
show a loss no real shop would accept.

Tuning target: the default view (2026, USPS commercial, default fuel, peak
off, flat $9.99) opens near break-even overall for the cheapest carrier (blended
margin within about $1 per parcel), with losses where they would be in reality.
Measured with the rate engine by ``--check`` (no engine or data change):

    200 rows, 307 parcels: 81 % under 5 lb, 7.2 % over 1 cu ft, 3.9 % two to
    three day, 1.0 % next day, 80 % residential, 2.3 % in delivery areas
    revenue $10.67 per parcel (flat $9.99 plus the expedited prices)
    USPS (cheapest): $10.98 per parcel, margin -$0.31 per parcel, 40 % of parcels at a loss
    UPS $31.14 and FedEx $31.22 per parcel (list prices, residential, fuel)
    best mix: all 307 parcels with USPS, same as USPS alone
    losses (USPS): bulky boxes -$10.69 per parcel (all at a loss), 5 to 20 lb
    -$6 to -$8, zones 5 to 8 -$1 to -$4 (about 65 % at a loss), next day
    -$4.41; gains: under 1 lb +$3.71, zones 1 to 4, two to three day +$8.22.
    USPS has no delivery area surcharge, so those parcels do not lose with USPS.

Regenerate and measure (fixed seed, reproducible):

    uv run --directory backend python scripts/make_sample_parcels.py
    uv run --directory backend python scripts/make_sample_parcels.py --check
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import random
import sys
from pathlib import Path

SEED = 20261023
N = 200
OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "app" / "sample_parcels.csv"
COLUMNS = [
    "weight_lb",
    "length_in",
    "width_in",
    "height_in",
    "distance_miles",
    "residential",
    "speed",
    "quantity",
    "price_charged",
    "delivery_area",
    "nonstandard_packaging",
]
CUBIC_FOOT = 1728

# (name, share of the non-bulky rows, weight range lb, box sizes in inches) — illustrative product mix.
PROFILES = [
    ("mailer", 0.55, (0.3, 2.0), [(9, 6, 2), (10, 8, 2), (10, 7, 4), (12, 9, 3)]),  # linens, small decor
    ("small box", 0.32, (2.0, 5.0), [(10, 8, 6), (12, 9, 4), (12, 10, 6), (12, 12, 6)]),  # mugs, candles
    ("medium box", 0.13, (5.0, 12.0), [(14, 12, 8), (16, 10, 8), (14, 14, 8)]),  # sets, cookware (< 1 cu ft)
```

+import { afterEach, describe, expect, it, vi } from "vitest";
+import { act, renderHook } from "@testing-library/react";
+import { useDebounced } from "./useDebounced";
+
+afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers());
+
+describe("useDebounced", () => {
+  it("settles on the last value once it stops changing for the delay", () => {
+    vi.useFakeTimers();
+    const { result, rerender } = renderHook(({ v }) => useDebounced(v, 250), { initialProps: { v: 1 } });
+    rerender({ v: 2 });
+    act(() => vi.advanceTimersByTime(200));
+    rerender({ v: 3 });
+    act(() => vi.advanceTimersByTime(200));
+    expect(result.current).toBe(1);
+    act(() => vi.advanceTimersByTime(50));
+    expect(result.current).toBe(3);
+  });
+
+  it("passes the value straight through with no delay", () => {
+    const { result, rerender } = renderHook(({ v }) => useDebounced(v, 0), { initialProps: { v: "a" } });
+    rerender({ v: "b" });
+    expect(result.current).toBe("b");
+  });
+});
diff --git a/frontend/src/hooks/useDebounced.ts b/frontend/src/hooks/useDebounced.ts
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..f37314f
--- /dev/null
+++ b/frontend/src/hooks/useDebounced.ts
@@ -0,0 +1,15 @@
+import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
+
+/** The value after it has stopped changing for `delayMs`; a delay of 0 or less passes it straight through. */
+export function useDebounced<T>(value: T, delayMs: number): T {
+  const [settled, setSettled] = useState(value);
+  useEffect(() => {
+    if (delayMs <= 0) {
+      setSettled(value);
+      return;
+    }
+    const t = setTimeout(() => setSettled(value), delayMs);
+    return () => clearTimeout(t);
+  }, [value, delayMs]);
+  return delayMs <= 0 ? value : settled;
+}

+

+
+export const carrierName = (c: Carrier | string) => CARRIER_NAME[c as Carrier] ?? c;

@@ -8,3 +14,31 @@ export const carrierWashVar = (c: Carrier) => `var(--carrier-${c}-wash)`;
 export function carrierColor(c: Carrier, el: Element = document.documentElement): string {
   return getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue(`--carrier-${c}`).trim();
 }
+
+/** Carriers that publish prices for `year`; all three when meta is not loaded yet. */
+export function carriersForYear(meta: Meta | null, year: number): Carrier[] {
+  if (!meta) return [...CARRIERS];
+  return CARRIERS.filter((c) => meta.years[c]?.includes(year));
+}
+
+/** "2027 prices are published by FedEx only" style sentence, or null when all three publish. */
+export function missingCarriersNote(available: Carrier[], year: number, names: Record<Carrier, string>): string | null {
+  if (available.length === CARRIERS.length) return null;
+  if (available.length === 0) return `No carrier has published ${year} prices in this data.`;
+  const list = available.map((c) => names[c]).join(" and ");
+  const missing = CARRIERS.filter((c) => !available.includes(c));
+  const missingList = missing.map((c) => names[c]).join(" and ");
+  const verb = missing.length === 1 ? "has" : "have";
+  const consequence = available.length === 1 ? "so there is nothing to compare against" : "so they are left out";
+  return `${year} prices are published by ${list} only. ${missingList} ${verb} not published ${year} prices yet, ${consequence}.`;
+}
+
+/** The service's display name from /api/meta, or a readable fallback built from its id. */
+export function serviceName(meta: Meta | null, serviceId: string): string {
+  const found = meta?.services.find((s) => s.service_id === serviceId);
+  if (found) return found.display_name;
+  return serviceId
+    .split("_")
+    .map((w) => (w === "usps" || w === "ups" ? w.toUpperCase() : w === "fedex" ? "FedEx" : w[0]!.toUpperCase() + w.slice(1)))
+    .join(" ");
+}

-export const CARRIER_NAME: Record<Carrier, string> = { usps: "USPS", ups: "UPS", fedex: "FedEx" };
+/** "+$1.23" / "−$1.23" (true minus sign), "$0.00" for zero. */
+export function signedUsd(n: number): string {
+  const r = Math.round(n * 100) / 100;
+  if (r === 0) return formatUsd(0);
+  return `${r > 0 ? "+" : "−"}${formatUsd(Math.abs(r))}`;
+}
+
+/** "+4.1%" / "−2.0%" with one decimal by default. */
+export function signedPct(n: number, digits = 1): string {
+  const r = Number(n.toFixed(digits));
+  if (r === 0) return `0${digits ? "." + "0".repeat(digits) : ""}%`;
+  return `${r > 0 ? "+" : "−"}${Math.abs(r).toFixed(digits)}%`;
+}
+
+/* ---------- margin: sign and word, never colour alone ---------- */
+
+/** Margins that round to $0.00 are break-even: no sign, no profit or loss colour. */
+const BREAK_EVEN = 0.005;
+const isBreakEven = (margin: number) => Math.abs(margin) < BREAK_EVEN;
+
+/** "+$1.58 margin" / "−$1.90 loss" / "$0.00, break-even". */
+export function marginText(margin: number): string {
+  if (isBreakEven(margin)) return "$0.00, break-even";
+  return margin > 0 ? `+${formatUsd(margin)} margin` : `−${formatUsd(-margin)} loss`;
+}
+
+/** Colour class that agrees with marginText: "is-loss", "is-profit", or none at break-even. */
+export const marginClass = (margin: number) => (isBreakEven(margin) ? "" : margin < 0 ? "is-loss" : "is-profit");
+
+/* ---------- labels ---------- */
+
 export const TIER_NAME: Record<Tier, string> = {
   ground: "Ground",
   two_three_day: "2–3 day",
   next_day: "Next day",
 };
+
+export const tierName = (t: string) => TIER_NAME[t as Tier] ?? t;
+
+/** Surcharge conditions (surcharges.csv) in the owner's words. */
+const CONDITION_LABEL: Record<string, string> = {
+  residential: "Home delivery",
+  delivery_area: "Remote area",
+  delivery_area_extended: "Extended remote area",
+  additional_handling_packaging: "Handling: packaging",
+  additional_handling_weight: "Handling: weight",
+  additional_handling_length: "Handling: length",
+  additional_handling_width: "Handling: width",
+  nonstandard_volume: "Non-standard size",
+  nonstandard_length: "Non-standard length",
+  oversize: "Oversize",
+};
+
+export function conditionLabel(condition: string): string {
+  return CONDITION_LABEL[condition] ?? condition.replace(/_/g, " ").replace(/^./, (c) => c.toUpperCase());
+}

````
1	# Parcel rates: USPS, UPS and FedEx list prices for a small online shop
2	
3	A dashboard that prices a shop's own parcels at the published prices of the
4	three US parcel carriers, for every year from 2023 to 2026, and shows which
5	carrier is cheapest, where the breakeven points are, how much of the bill is
6	surcharges, and how the cost moved year by year.
7	
8	## Run it
9	
10	Requires Docker with Compose v2. No accounts, keys or database setup.
11	
12	```sh
13	docker compose up --build
14	```
15	
16	Then open **http://localhost:8088**. The first build takes a minute or two.
17	Click "Load sample mix" to load an illustrative example parcel set, or upload your
18	own CSV (columns below). Stop with `Ctrl+C`, then `docker compose down`.
19	
20	Only port 8088 is published. nginx serves the built dashboard and proxies
21	`/api/` to the backend container, which is not reachable from the host. The
22	rate tables are baked into the backend image; the app never fetches anything
23	from the carriers at run time.
24	
25	## The problem and the user
26	
27	The user is the owner of a small online shop that sends a few hundred to a few
28	thousand parcels a month, has no negotiated carrier contract, and therefore
29	pays published prices. The carrier is usually chosen by habit, and the flat
30	shipping price charged to customers was set once and not revisited.
31	
32	The dashboard supports two decisions: which carrier and service to use for
33	each kind of parcel, and whether the flat shipping price still covers the real
34	cost once surcharges and yearly price increases are included.
35	
36	### What it answers
37	
38	| # | Question | The view |
39	|---|---|---|
40	| 1 | For one parcel (weight, size, distance, home or business, speed), which service is cheapest once surcharges are included, and what are the line items? | The cheapest total for the chosen speed comes first, with its saving over the next cheapest and the margin against your price. Below it, every carrier's cheapest service ranked, each with base rate, every surcharge (with its source page) and fuel. The form can start from one of your loaded parcels. |
41	| 2 | Where are the breakeven points between the Postal Service and FedEx or UPS ground, by weight and distance? | A weight by distance heatmap coloured by the cheapest ground carrier, for home or business delivery, with a heavy line where USPS stops winning and a plain-words readout of the breakeven weights; every cell's prices on hover, tap or focus, and the grid as a table. |
42	| 3 | For the whole parcel set, what is the blended cost per parcel with each carrier, and how much of it is surcharges? | The cheapest single carrier's cost per parcel and the "best mix" (cheapest carrier per parcel), then a yes or no on whether your shipping price covers the cost, the margin per parcel and the share shipped at a loss per carrier. A stacked chart (or table) splits the cost into base, the largest surcharges and fuel. Chips narrow everything to one kind of parcel (weight, distance, home or business, speed). |
43	| 4 | How did that blended cost change year by year, compared with the average increase the carriers announced, and which parcels drove it? | The cheapest carrier's change since the first year against the compounded announced increases, a year by year chart (dollars or index) with the announced path, how much of the biggest rise was fuel, the segments that drove each step, and a next-year slider that projects the cost. |
44	
45	Global controls: price year, USPS rate card, fuel surcharge override, peak
46	season toggle, and the flat price charged per parcel.
47	
48	Parcel CSV columns: `weight_lb, length_in, width_in, height_in,
49	distance_miles, residential, speed` (`ground`, `two_three_day`, `next_day`),
50	plus optional `quantity`, `price_charged`, `delivery_area`,
51	`nonstandard_packaging`. The full schema is in
52	[docs/data/SCHEMA.md](docs/data/SCHEMA.md).
53	
54	**The sample mix** is an illustrative home-goods shop, an example and not real
55	shipping data, generated by `backend/scripts/make_sample_parcels.py` with a
56	fixed seed: 200 rows, 307 parcels, mostly light ground parcels in boxes under
57	one cubic foot (about 80 % under 5 lb), about 7 % bulky boxes over one cubic
58	foot, 4 % two to three day and 1 % next day, about 80 % to homes, distances
59	weighted toward the middle zones, and a handful in delivery areas. Ground rows
60	leave `price_charged` empty and use the flat price control; expedited rows
61	carry what a shop would charge at checkout, $19.99 for two to three day and
62	$39.99 for next day, because real shops charge more for faster shipping. At the
63	default controls (2026, USPS commercial, $9.99) the mix opens near break-even:
64	USPS, the cheapest carrier, costs $10.98 per parcel against $10.67 charged on
65	average (−$0.31 per parcel), and the 40 % of parcels shipped at a loss are
66	mostly the bulky boxes, parcels over 5 lb and the far zones.
67	
68	## Data provenance
69	
70	All prices come from the carriers' own published rate documents:
71	
72	| Carrier | Base rates | Surcharge rules | Years |
73	|---|---|---|---|
74	| USPS | Postal Explorer CSV zips per price change; Notice 123 PDFs | Notice 123 footnotes; Domestic Mail Manual for dimensional weight | 2023 (July tables, Ground Advantage launch) to 2026 |
75	| UPS | Daily Rates guide PDF per year | Surcharge section of the same guide; demand surcharge PDFs | 2023 to 2026 |
76	| FedEx | Standard List Rates XLSX (PDF for 2023 and 2024) | Yearly surcharge-change PDFs and Service Guides | 2023 to 2026, plus 2027 as a forward year |
77	
78	**Collection.** Every raw file is listed in
79	[data/raw/manifest.csv](data/raw/manifest.csv) with its URL, retrieval method,
80	SHA-256 and size, and each carrier folder has a `SOURCES.md` describing what
81	each file is. `python3 data/fetch_raw.py` restores missing files one at a
82	time, with a pause and jitter between requests, backoff on errors, an
83	identifying User-Agent and checksum verification. UPS and FedEx block direct
84	downloads from scripts, so 78 of the 135 files are fetched through the Wayback
85	Machine (`method=wayback`).
86	
87	**What is committed.** Spreadsheets, CSV zips and small HTML snapshots (58
88	files, about 9 MB) are in git. The PDFs (77 files, about 137 MB) are not; run
89	`python3 data/fetch_raw.py` to get them. The processed tables in
90	`data/processed/` are committed, so the app and the backend tests never need
91	the raw files.
92	
93	**Regenerating `data/processed/`** (needs the PDFs, so fetch first):
94	
95	```sh
96	python3 data/fetch_raw.py                     # standard library only
97	uv run python -m data.pipeline.usps
98	uv run python -m data.pipeline.ups
99	uv run python -m data.pipeline.fedex
100	uv run python -m data.pipeline.report_changes # rewrites docs/data/RULE_CHANGES.md
101	```
102	
103	Base rates are parsed. Surcharges, fuel defaults, announced increases,
104	dimensional weight rules and the distance-to-zone bands are curated by hand
105	in `data/pipeline/*_rules.py`, each row with the source file, page and a
106	verbatim quote. Details: [docs/data/QUALITY.md](docs/data/QUALITY.md) (survey
107	and decisions), [docs/data/SCHEMA.md](docs/data/SCHEMA.md) (tables) and
108	[docs/data/RULE_CHANGES.md](docs/data/RULE_CHANGES.md) (every rule that
109	changed between years).
110	
111	### Rate cards
112	
113	| Carrier | Card | What it is |
114	|---|---|---|
115	| USPS | `commercial` (default) | Price paid with online postage or shipping software; no contract or volume needed |
116	| USPS | `retail` | Price paid at the Post Office counter |
117	| UPS | `list` | Published Daily Rates, what a shipper without a contract pays |
118	| FedEx | `list` | Published Standard List Rates, same meaning |
119	
120	Commercial is the USPS default because a small online seller buys labels
121	through a marketplace or shipping software, which gives commercial prices to
122	anyone. Comparing UPS and FedEx list prices against USPS retail would
123	overstate what the shop pays the Postal Service. The retail card is one switch
124	away in the controls.
125	
126	## Key choices
127	
128	- **Stack.** Python 3.12, FastAPI and Pydantic for the rate engine and API,
129	  managed with `uv`. Vite, React and TypeScript for the dashboard, Recharts
130	  for line and bar charts and a hand-drawn SVG heatmap. Two containers behind
131	  one `docker compose` command. Reasons and alternatives are in
132	  [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md).
133	- **CSV in memory, no database.** The rate tables are about 40,000 rows of
134	  committed CSV, loaded once at startup. Nothing to configure.
135	- **Curated rules with tested citations.** Surcharge prose in PDFs is too
136	  irregular to parse reliably, so the amounts were transcribed by hand. A test
137	  opens each cited page and checks that the quote, including the amount, is
138	  there.
139	- **Golden cells.** `data/tests/golden/<carrier>_<year>.csv` holds price cells
140	  checked by hand against the documents, including the corners of every
141	  table; the parsed output must match them exactly.
142	- **Time-varying rules.** Every rule carries `effective_from` and an inclusive
143	  `effective_to`, and a quote is priced on an `as_of` date. This handles
144	  mid-year changes such as the USPS dimensional divisor moving from 166 to 139
145	  on 2026-07-12, peak windows and the 2026 USPS transportation surcharge.
146	- **Ledger design.** The answer to each question is the largest thing in its
147	  section; assumptions sit in a quiet side rail. See
148	  [frontend/DESIGN.md](frontend/DESIGN.md).
149	
150	## Known limitations
151	
152	- List prices only: a shipper with a negotiated contract pays less.
153	- Zones are estimated from distance bands, not looked up from ZIP code pairs.
154	- The UPS fuel surcharge default is a proxy taken from FedEx's published
155	  history (no UPS history is retrievable); the slider overrides it.
156	- UPS announced increases come from trade press, not from UPS itself.
157	- UPS peak (demand) surcharge documents for the 2025-26 and 2026-27 seasons
158	  are not in the sources, so UPS 2025 and 2026 peak quotes carry no peak
159	  charges.
160	- FedEx 2027 surcharges are incomplete (only the Home Delivery residential
161	  charge and January peak rows), so 2027 totals understate surcharges.
162	- Peak surcharges are a toggle that prices on December 10 of the year, not by
163	  ship date.
164	- UPS and FedEx bill a large or oversize package at a minimum of 90 lb. That
165	  minimum is not modelled, so the base rate of such parcels is understated;
166	  the surcharge itself is included (issue #18).
167	- Weight is capped at 70 lb, the USPS maximum. Alaska and Hawaii are out of
168	  scope.
169	- UPS 2024 and 2026 use the mid-year revision of the Daily Rates guide,
170	  because the December original could not be retrieved.
171	
172	The same list is returned by `GET /api/meta` and shown in the app.
173	
174	## What I would improve next
175	
176	Open issues in the repository, in rough priority order:
177	
178	- #18 model the 90 lb minimum billable weight for large and oversize packages.
179	- #14 capture the UPS 2025-26 and 2026-27 demand surcharge documents.
180	- #9 real ZIP-to-ZIP zones instead of distance bands.
181	- #10 per-parcel price column and order-value shipping rules (free shipping
182	  over a threshold).
183	- #11 next-year projection from announced increases.
184	- #13 script the source discovery so data collection runs end to end without
185	  an agent.
186	- #8 Playwright end-to-end tests at desktop and phone widths.
187	
188	## Local development without Docker
189	
190	Needs Python 3.12 with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and Node 18.18 or
191	newer (the image uses Node 22).
192	
193	```sh
194	# backend on http://localhost:8787
195	cd backend && uv run uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8787
196	
197	# frontend on http://localhost:5173, proxies /api to localhost:8787
198	cd frontend && npm ci && npm run dev
199	```
200	
201	`VITE_API_TARGET` points the dev proxy elsewhere. `http://localhost:5173/?mock=1`
202	runs the frontend alone on recorded API responses. The API contract is in
203	[docs/API.md](docs/API.md), with example payloads in `docs/api-examples/`
204	(regenerated by `uv run --directory backend python scripts/export_api_examples.py`).
205	
206	## Tests
207	
208	| Suite | Command | What it covers |
209	|---|---|---|
210	| Data | `ALLOW_MISSING_RAW=1 uv run pytest` (repository root) | Schema, parsers against golden cells, table invariants, manifest, citations |
211	| Data, full | `python3 data/fetch_raw.py && uv run pytest` | Same, with every citation checked against its PDF page |
212	| Backend | `cd backend && uv run pytest` | Rate engine against hand-computed quotes, rule resolution, analysis and API |
213	| Frontend | `cd frontend && npm ci && npm test` | Components with Testing Library and the API contract test |
214	| Frontend types | `cd frontend && npm run typecheck` | |
215	
216	Without the PDFs, the citation and PDF parser tests fail with a message
217	telling you to fetch them; `ALLOW_MISSING_RAW=1` skips them on purpose
218	instead. End-to-end Playwright tests come with issue #8.
219	
220	## Repository layout
221	
222	```
223	backend/            FastAPI app (app/), tests, scripts; Dockerfile
224	frontend/           Vite + React dashboard; Dockerfile and nginx config
225	data/raw/           manifest.csv, SOURCES.md per carrier, committed raw files
226	data/pipeline/      parsers and curated rules that write data/processed/
227	data/processed/     the rate tables the app loads
228	data/tests/         data tests and golden cells
229	docs/               decisions, API contract, data docs, agent log
230	docker-compose.yml  the reviewer run path
231	```
232	
233	## How this was built: the agent log
234	
235	The project was built with Claude Code, one GitHub issue per task, each in its
236	own branch and git worktree, merged through pull requests. Every session and
237	subagent transcript is exported to [docs/agent-log/](docs/agent-log/) as
238	Markdown by a `SessionEnd` hook (`.claude/hooks/export-session.sh`), with the
239	prompts, the agent's responses and its tool calls. Home directory paths are
240	redacted. [docs/DECISIONS.md](docs/DECISIONS.md) is the running log of the
241	decisions those conversations led to.
242	
````

</details>

Build an analytical dashboard with an AI coding agent

This exercise gives us a concrete project to discuss: the problem you chose, what your dashboard helps a user learn, and how you worked with an agent and Git to reach a presentable MVP. The project is intentionally open ended so we can see your judgment.

# About Intelligent Audit

Intelligent Audit helps shippers understand and control transportation costs. Our technology audits freight and parcel invoices, identifies billing discrepancies, and turns shipping data into insights for better decisions. Your project does not need to use logistics data; choose a problem you find compelling.

# The assignment

Choose a real problem or decision that interests you, find or create a suitable dataset, and build an analytical dashboard that helps a specific user explore it. Explain who that user is and what questions the dashboard answers. Use an AI coding agent as part of your workflow. The finished application must run in Docker and be usable by a reviewer on a local machine.

Aim for roughly three to five hours of focused work. Stop when you have an MVP you would be comfortable demonstrating. We do not expect a production system, a polished design system, or an exhaustive dataset. You do not need to exhaust your agent’s token allowance; we care about the choices you make within a reasonable timebox.

# What to build

- Use Python for a substantive part of the project, such as data collection, processing, analysis, or the backend. The dashboard itself may use another language, such as TypeScript, if that helps you create a more feature rich and visually polished experience. Present useful analysis rather than raw records or unexplained charts, with meaningful metrics and at least one way to filter, segment, or aggregate the data.

- A clearly defined problem, audience, and data source. State the main insight or decision the dashboard is meant to support, and note important data limitations.

- A Dockerfile and, if needed, a Docker Compose file. A reviewer should be able to start the app with the exact command in your README and open it at a documented local URL.

- A small, reproducible dataset or a dependable data setup path. If the app normally fetches external data, provide a local sample or fallback so the review does not depend on a live service.

# Your development process

Commit your work to a Git repository with a history that shows the project evolving. We will read the commits, so use descriptive messages and commit at meaningful points rather than submitting a single final snapshot.

Commit a readable record of the prompts and interactions with your coding agent in the repository, for example under docs/agent-log/. An export or chronological Markdown log is fine. Include your prompts, the agent’s substantive responses, and enough context to connect major decisions or code changes to the conversation. If your tool cannot export a full transcript, reconstruct the relevant exchanges faithfully and say so. Remove API keys, credentials, personal information, and unrelated private context before committing. You do not need to provide hidden model reasoning.

# Submission

- Share a repository link or an archive that preserves the complete Git history, including the agent interaction log.

- In README.md, give the one or two commands to run the app, the local URL, the problem and intended user, data provenance, key choices, known limitations, and what you would improve next.

## 2026-10-22 — Problem, user and scope

**Problem.** A small online shop sends a few hundred to a few thousand parcels
a month, has no negotiated carrier contract, and pays the published list
prices of FedEx, UPS and the Postal Service. Today the carrier is chosen by
habit. The dashboard helps the owner choose the carrier per kind of parcel,
and check whether the flat shipping price charged to customers still covers
the real cost once surcharges and yearly price increases are included.

**Questions the dashboard answers.**

1. For a given parcel (weight, dimensions, distance, residential or business,
   required speed), which service is cheapest once surcharges are included,
   and what are the line items of that price?
2. Where are the breakeven points between the Postal Service and FedEx or UPS
   ground, by weight and distance?
3. For the owner's whole set of parcels, what is the blended cost per parcel
   with each carrier, and how much of it is surcharges rather than base rate?
4. How did that blended cost change year by year under each year's published
   prices, compared with the average increase the carriers announced, and
   which kinds of parcels in the mix drove the change?

**Scope decisions.**

- Timebox: issues are sized to fit about five hours of focused work (the
  brief's upper bound). Extras are tracked separately and only started if
  time remains. Time actually spent is recorded by the owner, not estimated.
- Services: three speed tiers across the three carriers — ground, two to
  three day, and next day. Weight capped at 70 lb (the USPS maximum).
- Years covered: decided after the data survey (issue 1), based on what can

## Price Changes Overview

USPS proposed price increases of approximately 6.6 percent for Priority Mail service, 5.1 percent for Priority Mail Express service, 7.8 percent for USPS Ground Advantage and 6.0 percent for Parcel Select, which took effect January 18, 2026.

## Current Pricing Information

Priority Mail Express retail and commercial prices remained the same as of July 12, 2026, Priority Mail retail and commercial prices remained the same, and USPS Ground Advantage retail prices remained the same.

## CSV Files Availability

CSV files are available for USPS Ground Advantage and Priority Mail – Retail pricing. These files can be accessed through the USPS website at https://www.usps.com/business/prices.htm.

Additionally, as of September 18, 2026, Time-Limited 2026 Price Files in CSV format are available as Final status documents on the Postal Explorer website (pe.usps.com/PriceChange), which includes pricing information effective October 4, 2026 through January 17, 2027.

Based on my search results, I found information about USPS nonstandard fees and dimensional weight pricing:

## Key Findings:

**Dimensional Weight Divisor:**
The divisor is 139 as of July 12, 2026, down from 166, and applies to Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, USPS Ground Advantage, and Parcel Select packages larger than 1 cubic foot.

**Nonstandard Fees for USPS Ground Advantage:**
A USPS Ground Advantage mailpiece is subject to a nonstandard fee for packages more than 22 inches up to 30 inches long, more than 30 inches long, or more than 2 cubic feet (3,456 cubic inches).

**Zone Applicability:**
It's important to note that there are different rules depending on zones. Dimensional weight applies when package volume exceeds 1,728 cubic inches and destination is in Zones 5 through 9, with a divisor of 166. However, this appears to be older information; the more recent July 2026 guidance indicates the divisor changed to 139 for zones 1-9.

**Cubic Foot Threshold:**
Dimensional weight rates apply to domestic packages larger than 1 cubic foot (1,728 cubic inches).

The search results indicate that USPS's official sources at pe.usps.com contain the most current information as of July 2026.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding USPS temporary price changes for peak holiday shipping seasons:

## 2026 Holiday Shipping Season

The U.S. Postal Service filed notice with the Postal Regulatory Commission regarding a temporary price change for some package products for the 2026 peak holiday season. The higher prices are in effect from October 4, 2026, through January 17, 2027.

The planned change would affect prices on Priority Mail Express (PME), Priority Mail (PM), USPS Ground Advantage, and Parcel Select. The temporary price adjustment is to help cover extra handling costs to ensure a successful peak season.

## 2025 Holiday Shipping Season

The U.S. Postal Service filed notice regarding a temporary price change for some package services for the 2025 peak holiday season, as a temporary price adjustment to help cover extra handling costs to ensure a successful peak season. The temporary rates would go into effect at midnight Central on Oct. 5 and remain in place until midnight Central on Jan. 18, 2026.

## How USPS Differs from Other Carriers

USPS does not use the word "surcharge." It files a temporary price change with the Postal Regulatory Commission, and the higher prices simply become the prices for the season.

USPS implemented a time-limited price increase of 8% to its Retail and Commercial domestic shipping rates starting April 26, 2026, through January 17, 2027. 

USPS states this is a temporary adjustment aimed at better aligning shipping rates with current transportation costs, helping ensure pricing reflects today's market conditions.

The change includes an 8% increase to base postage rates for select domestic competitive products like Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, USPS Ground Advantage, and Parcel Select.

Specifically for Ground Advantage, most Ground Advantage rates are increasing an average of 7.8%, but like Priority Mail, the price changes are complex and depend on zone and weight of the package. However, this 7.8% figure is from the January 18, 2026 change—the April 26 change applies an additional 8% temporary surcharge on top of that.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about the USPS temporary price changes for the 2024 holiday shipping season.

The U.S. Postal Service filed notice with the Postal Regulatory Commission (PRC) regarding a temporary price change for some package services for the 2024 peak holiday season. The planned peak-season pricing, which was approved by the governors of the Postal Service on Aug. 8, would affect prices on the following commercial and retail domestic competitive parcels: Priority Mail Express (PME), Priority Mail (PM) and USPS Ground Advantage.

Pending favorable review by the PRC, the temporary rates would go into effect at midnight Central on Oct. 6 and remain in place until midnight Central on Jan. 19, 2025. This temporary price adjustment is to help cover extra handling costs to ensure a successful peak season.

The search results include detailed pricing information for various weight zones and package types. For example, for USPS Ground Advantage in Zones 5-9, there would be a $0.35 increase for 0-3 lbs, $0.75 increase for 4-10 lbs, $1.25 increase for 11-25 lbs, and $5.50 increase for 26-70 lbs.

The official announcement was made on September 5, 2024, via the USPS newsroom at about.usps.com.

Based on the search results, here's information about USPS's July 2026 price changes for shipping services:

## Key Changes Effective July 12, 2026

On July 12, 2026, USPS changed how packages are priced rather than raising base rates across the board.

### Percent Changes in 2026

Earlier in 2026, USPS implemented percent increases that set the stage for July's changes:

- USPS Ground Advantage experienced a 7.8% average rate increase (January 2026)
- Priority Mail's average price increased to 6.6%, and Priority Mail Express rose an average of 5.1% (January 2026)
- Additionally, there was an 8% increase on domestic services like Priority Mail, Priority Mail Express, USPS Ground Advantage, and Parcel Select (April 26, 2026)

### July 12, 2026 Specific Changes

The July changes focused on structural modifications rather than base rate increases:

- Priority Mail Express retail and commercial prices remained the same, as did Priority Mail retail and commercial prices
- USPS Ground Advantage retail prices remained the same
- The dimensional weight divisor dropped from 166 to 139 for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, USPS Ground Advantage, and Parcel Select, raising the billable weight of every dim-rated package by roughly 19%
- The Postal Service revised USPS Ground Advantage – Commercial ounce price points to reflect the same price for each ounce price point within a zone

## 2023 Holiday Season (October 1, 2023)

I was unable to locate a specific announcement dated October 1, 2023 regarding temporary price changes for the 2023 holiday season in the search results. The 2023 results focus primarily on regular pricing changes that took effect July 9, 2023, rather than temporary peak-season adjustments.

## 2022 Peak Season (October 2, 2022)

The United States Postal Service filed notice with the Postal Regulatory Commission (PRC) regarding a temporary price adjustment for key package products for the 2022 peak holiday season. Pending favorable review by the PRC, the temporary rates would go into effect at 12 a.m. Central on Oct. 2, and remain in place until 12 a.m. Central Jan. 22, 2023.

The planned peak-season pricing would affect prices on the following commercial and retail domestic competitive parcels: Priority Mail Express (PME), Priority Mail (PM), First-Class Package Service (FCPS), Parcel Select and USPS Retail Ground.

The 2022 temporary price changes included specific increases for different service types and weight zones, with rates approved by the Postal Regulatory Commission on September 8, 2022.

Based on my web searches, I have found information about the USPS price changes for both July 2022 and July 2023. Let me provide you with the results:

## July 2022 Price Change (Effective July 10, 2022)

The United States Postal Service filed notice with the Postal Regulatory Commission (PRC) of price changes to take effect July 10, 2022. However, I was unable to find specific percentage increase information for Priority Mail and Priority Mail Express products in the July 2022 rate change from the USPS newsroom documents. The search results show information about January 2022 rate changes (which included 3.1% increases for both Priority Mail and Priority Mail Express), but not the specific percentages for the July 2022 competitive products rate change.

The July 2022 change involved adjustments to competitive products including Priority Mail and Priority Mail Express, but the exact percentage increases are not clearly stated in the available search results from the USPS newsroom.

## July 2023 Ground Advantage Launch Price Change

The USPS announced on June 27 that it had received approval from the Postal Regulatory Commission (PRC) to launch USPS Ground Advantage on July 9, 2023.

Published prices for USPS Ground Advantage will decrease 1.4 percent compared with current Parcel Select Ground and First-Class Package Service pricing. USPS Ground Advantage retail prices will decrease 3.2 percent, and USPS Ground Advantage Commercial published prices will decrease 0.7 percent.

For the specific percentage changes for Priority Mail and Priority Mail Express in July 2022, you may need to access the detailed price change tables directly from the Postal Explorer website (pe.usps.com/PriceChange/Index) or the Federal Register notices referenced in the USPS newsroom announcements.

Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about the USPS July 12, 2026 price change and dimensional weight update:

## Key Changes Effective July 12, 2026

**Dimensional Weight Divisor Change:**
USPS Dimensional Weight Divisor will change from 166 to 139. This matches the divisor UPS and FedEx already use, and it raises the billable weight of every dim-rated package by roughly 19%.

**Which Services Are Affected:**
It applies to Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, USPS Ground Advantage, and Parcel Select packages larger than 1 cubic foot.

**New Dimension Requirements:**
Starting July 12, 2026, USPS requires length, width, and height on all commercial parcel manifests. As of this date, rating requests missing required dimensions will return an error.

**Rounding Changes:**
USPS calculates dimensional weight by dividing a package's volume by 139 instead of 166, and rounds every fractional inch up instead of to the nearest inch.

**Noncompliance Fees:**
USPS will charge a $3.00 per parcel Dimension Noncompliance Fee for any package with missing or incorrect dimensions. However, USPS has deferred assessment of its Dimension Noncompliance fee until Phase Two (early 2027, tentative).

**Other Changes:**
Published Commercial USPS Ground Advantage prices will no longer use ounce-based rate differentiation.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding USPS and peak season surcharges for the 2023 holiday season:

## USPS No Peak Season Surcharges Announcement

On September 19, 2023, USPS announced it would not be assessing peak season surcharges for the 2023 holiday season. This ended a practice that began in 2020.

## Ground Advantage Connection

USPS wanted to try and pull market share with their new USPS Ground Advantage program. USPS Ground Advantage is a service that provides a simple, reliable and affordable way to ship packages with day certain delivery of 2-5 business days based on distance.

## Reasoning Behind the Decision

Officials credited more workers moving into long-term, career positions and network investments with helping the Postal Service reduce holiday operating expenses and nixing the need for peak surcharges. This was made possible by USPS converting nearly 150,000 employees to full-time, career roles.

## No Additional Fees

The Postal Service announced it will not levy any additional surcharges for customers this holiday season, offering increased predictability in pricing. There were no additional fees for residential area delivery, for Saturday delivery or for minimum volumes.

I found relevant information about USPS price changes and dimensional weight updates for July 2026. Here are the key findings:

## USPS Price Changes Filing (May 2026)

On May 11, 2026, the U.S. Postal Service notified the Postal Regulatory Commission of recommended price changes for certain domestic competitive package and service offerings, also slated to take effect July 12.

## Dimensional Weight Changes

The Postal Service will align the divisor for dimensional weight pieces to industry standards for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, USPS Ground Advantage, and Parcel Select. Specifically, dimensional weighting will have its dim divisor changed from 166 to 139 to better align with industry standard.

## Additional Changes

The recommendation includes eliminating ounce-based rate differentiation for published Commercial USPS Ground Advantage prices, which USPS says will not affect customers with negotiated commercial rates, plus a 3 percent increase for competitive PO Box pricing. USPS also plans to introduce an Addresses API offering, align the dimensional weight divisor to industry standards for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, USPS Ground Advantage and Parcel Select and add new hazardous materials handling fees for Priority Mail Express and Priority Mail along with a noncompliance fee for improperly prepared hazardous materials shipped using competitive package products.

## PRC Approval

On May 27, 2026, the Postal Regulatory Commission (PRC) approved USPS' proposed pricing changes, which will take effect July 12, 2026.

cd ~/parcel-rates-issue-1 && cat > data/raw/usps/SOURCES.md <<'EOF'
# USPS raw sources — data-availability survey (retrieved 2026-10-22)

Carrier: USPS, domestic **retail** (published, non-contract) list prices.
Scope asked: 2022–2026, services Ground Advantage (since 2023-07-09; before that First-Class Package
Service / Parcel Select Ground / USPS Retail Ground), Priority Mail, Priority Mail Express, zones 1–9.

All downloads were made directly from the live USPS sites with `curl -A "Mozilla/5.0 ..."`.
Note: pe.usps.com returns HTTP 404 to clients without a browser-like User-Agent and to HTTP
range requests; with a UA every file below came back 200. The Wayback Machine CDX index
(`web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=pe.usps.com/resources/PriceChange/*`) was used only to
*discover* the exact file names of older price-change zips; the files themselves were then
fetched from pe.usps.com directly (not from Wayback).

Price-change calendar covered (effective dates, from the PDFs' cover pages / DMM archive folder dates):
2022-01-09, 2022-07-10, 2022-10-02 (peak), 2023-01-22, 2023-07-09 (Ground Advantage launch),
2024-01-21, 2024-07-14, 2024-10-06 (peak), 2025-01-19, 2025-07-13, 2025-10-05 (peak),
2026-01-18, 2026-04-26 (transportation-related time-limited), 2026-07-12, 2026-10-04 (peak).
There was **no** USPS peak price change in autumn 2023 (see press release 2023-09-19 below).

## A. Notice 123 "Price List" PDFs (one per price change)

Source pattern: `https://pe.usps.com/Archive/PDF/DMMArchive<YYYYMMDD>/Notice123.pdf` (DMM archive,
folder date = effective date), except the current one (`https://pe.usps.com/cpim/ftp/manuals/dmm300/notice123.pdf`)
and the April 2026 one (`https://pe.usps.com/resources/PriceChange/Transportation-Related%20Time-Limited%202026%20Price%20Change%20-%20Notice123%20PDF.pdf`).
Method: direct download. Format: PDF, 62–76 pages, text-based (not scanned).

Contents (all of them): domestic retail and commercial price tables for Priority Mail Express,
Priority Mail, Ground Advantage (2023-07 onward) / First-Class Package Service + USPS Retail Ground +
Parcel Select Ground (2022 and 2023-01), by zone 1–9 (zone 9 = Hawaii/Alaska-type) and weight
(Priority Mail / PME: 1–70 lb by pound; Ground Advantage retail: ounces up to 15.999 oz then pounds to 70 lb;
FCPS 2022: ounces to 15.999 oz), flat-rate prices, extra services, fees. Footnotes under each table
carry the surcharge rules (see section D).

Parse difficulty: PDF tables with footnotes printed in a right-hand column *beside* the table
(pdftotext -layout interleaves footnote text with price rows); tables for one product span
one or two pages. pdfplumber/camelot should work but the CSV zips (section B) are far easier —
use the PDFs for the footnote rules and as a cross-check only.

| File | URL | Effective |
|---|---|---|
| 2022/notice123_2022-01-09.pdf | https://pe.usps.com/Archive/PDF/DMMArchive20220109/Notice123.pdf | 2022-01-09 |

## B. Price-file CSV zips (Postal Explorer "Price Files – CSV" / "Notice 123.zip")

Method: direct download from `https://pe.usps.com/resources/PriceChange/<name>` (names below).
Format: ZIP of ~50 CSV files (one per product). Relevant retail files inside each zip:
`PM Retail.csv`, `PME Retail.csv`, and `USPS Ground Advantage Retail.csv` (2023-07 onward) /
`FCPS.csv`, `USPS Retail Ground.csv`, `Parcel Select Ground.csv` (2022-01 … 2023-01).
Also `PM Comm.csv`, `PME Comm.csv`, `USPS Ground Advantage Comm.csv` (commercial, out of scope).

Layout (checked on 2026-10-04 zip): a 1–2 line title row (`Priority Mail - Retail,,Final,,9/14/2026`),
flat-rate rows, then a header `Weight Not Over (Lbs),Zones` / `,Zone 1,…,Zone 9` followed by one row
per weight step (ounces for Ground Advantage: 4, 8, 12, 15.999; then pounds 1–70). ~90 lines per file.
Parse difficulty: **clean CSV, but with irregular preamble rows** — locate the `Zone 1` header row
programmatically, then read the numeric block; a float like `15.999000000000001` appears for the
15.999-oz step. Surcharge footnotes are NOT in the CSVs (they are only in the PDF).

## D. Surcharge rules (what the fetched documents say)

From the Notice 123 PDFs (footnotes beside the Priority Mail / PME / Ground Advantage tables):
- Nonstandard length fees: "Parcels that exceed 22 inches but not greater than 30 inches in length, add $…" and
  "Parcels that exceed 30 inches in length, add $…". Over-30-in amounts seen: $15.00 (2022-01, "Effective April 3, 2022"), $15.00 (2023-07),
  $18.00 (2025-01), $21.00 (2026-07 and 2026-10). Ground Advantage over-30-in: $7.00 (2023-07), $8.40 (2025-01), $10.00 (2026).
- Volume fee: "Parcels that exceed 2 cubic feet (3456 cubic inches), add $…": $15.00 (2022), $25.00 (2023-07 PM/PME),
  $35.00 (2026 PM/PME), $21.00 (2026 Ground Advantage).
  The 22–30 in amounts are in the same footnotes; read them per year from the PDF (not extracted here).
- Dimensional weight: every year's footnote says "Parcels that exceed one cubic foot (1,728 cubic inches) are charged based on
  the actual weight or the dimensional weight, whichever is greater". The divisor and the zone scope are NOT stated in
  Notice 123 (it refers to DMM 123/223). Web summaries say divisor 166 through 2026-07-11 and 139 from 2026-07-12 for
  PME/PM/GA/Parcel Select (the 2026-05-11 press release confirms a divisor change "to industry standards" but does not
  print the number) — **divisor values and zone applicability (zones 1–4 vs 5–9 in earlier years) are unverified from
  saved files; source DMM 123.1.6 / 223.1.6 for the year in question**.
- Residential / delivery-area surcharges: none found in any Notice 123 or press release; the 2023-09-19 release explicitly
  says no extra fees for residential delivery or Saturday delivery. USPS has no such surcharge for retail parcels (consistent
  with all fetched docs; absence-of-evidence only).
- Peak season: temporary price changes replace the base tables (prices in the "_peak" PDFs/zips are the full tables, not an
  add-on). Windows: 2022-10-02→2023-01-22; none in 2023; 2024-10-06→2025-01-19; 2025-10-05→2026-01-18; 2026-10-04→2027-01-17.
  2026 additionally has the 2026-04-26→2027-01-17 transportation-related increase stacked under the peak prices.

## E. Zone chart

- zones/postalpro_zone_charts_page.html — https://postalpro.usps.com/operations/zone-charts (scraped HTML, 2026-10-22).
  Links to: Domestic Zone Chart tool, "Zone Charts Matrix Technical Guide" (/national-zone-charts-matrix/ZoneChartsMatrixTechnicalGuide,
  effective June 2024 — the link returned an HTML page, not a PDF, so it was not kept), "Zone Charts Order Form" (/Zone_Charts_Order_Form,
  dated 2026-07-12), Zone 10 test files. The full National Zone Charts Matrix (origin ZIP3 x destination ZIP3 → zone) is
  obtained via the order form, not as an open bulk download on that page.
- zones/postcalc_domestic_zone_chart_page.html — https://postcalc.usps.com/DomesticZoneChart (scraped HTML). Form-driven tool:
  given an origin ZIP3 it returns the zone for every destination ZIP3 range (with "same NDC" and 5-digit exceptions), optionally as
  an Excel-formatted table; endpoints seen in the page: `/DomesticZoneChart/GetZoneChart` and `/DomesticZoneChart/GetZone`
  (POST form, chart date selectable). That is the practical free source: ~1,000 ZIP3 requests build the full matrix.
  Zones are distance-based (DMM 608.9 ranges; zone 9 = non-contiguous/territories); not verified here beyond the page text.

# Decisions

Running log of the choices made for this project, in the order they were made.
Each entry says what was decided, the alternatives considered, and why.
See `docs/ASSIGNMENT.md` for the brief and `docs/agent-log/` for the agent
conversations that led here.

## 2026-10-22 — Problem, user and scope

**Problem.** A small online shop sends a few hundred to a few thousand parcels
a month, has no negotiated carrier contract, and pays the published list
prices of FedEx, UPS and the Postal Service. Today the carrier is chosen by
habit. The dashboard helps the owner choose the carrier per kind of parcel,
and check whether the flat shipping price charged to customers still covers
the real cost once surcharges and yearly price increases are included.

**Questions the dashboard answers.**

1. For a given parcel (weight, dimensions, distance, residential or business,
   required speed), which service is cheapest once surcharges are included,
   and what are the line items of that price?
2. Where are the breakeven points between the Postal Service and FedEx or UPS
   ground, by weight and distance?
3. For the owner's whole set of parcels, what is the blended cost per parcel
   with each carrier, and how much of it is surcharges rather than base rate?
4. How did that blended cost change year by year under each year's published
   prices, compared with the average increase the carriers announced, and
   which kinds of parcels in the mix drove the change?

**Scope decisions.**

- Timebox: issues are sized to fit about five hours of focused work (the
  brief's upper bound). Extras are tracked separately and only started if
  time remains. Time actually spent is recorded by the owner, not estimated.
- Services: three speed tiers across the three carriers — ground, two to
  three day, and next day. Weight capped at 70 lb (the USPS maximum).
- Years covered: decided after the data survey (issue 1), based on what can
  actually be downloaded and parsed reliably.
- Parcel input: CSV upload plus a bundled illustrative sample mix. Columns:
  weight, length, width, height, distance in miles, residential flag,
  required speed, and an optional per-parcel price charged to the customer.
  Dimensional weight is computed from the dimensions.
- Price charged to the customer: a single flat price is the MVP control. The
  optional per-parcel column overrides it when present.
- Fuel and peak surcharges: a documented per-year default taken from the
  published history, a slider to stress test the fuel percentage, and a peak
  season toggle. A next-year increase slider sits on the year-over-year view.
- Zone from distance: a documented distance-band to zone mapping. Real
  ZIP-to-ZIP zones are a bonus, not MVP.
- The app never fetches live data; all rate tables are committed.

## 2026-10-22 — Stack

| Area | Decision | Alternatives considered | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backend | FastAPI, Pydantic models, pandas over committed CSV tables loaded in memory, managed with `uv` | DuckDB; SQLite | Rate cards are a few thousand rows. No database keeps Docker and setup trivial. |
| Data collection | Python scripts under `data/` that download the carriers' published rate documents, parse them (pdfplumber for PDFs), and write normalized CSVs that are committed | Hand-typed tables | Reproducible, documents provenance, and qualifies for the scraping bonus. |
| Frontend | Vite + React + TypeScript, Recharts for line and bar charts, a custom SVG heatmap for the breakeven map, plain CSS with design tokens | Chart.js (needs a matrix plugin for heatmaps); Plotly (over 1 MB, poor on mobile); Tailwind | Small bundle, declarative, the heatmap is a trivial grid. |
| Docker | `docker compose` with two services: uvicorn backend and an nginx container serving the Vite build and proxying `/api` | Single multi-stage image with FastAPI serving static files | Clean separation, one command for the reviewer. |
| Tests | pytest for pipeline, rate engine and API; Vitest + Testing Library for components; Playwright end to end at 1440 and 375 px with screenshots reviewed for UX | — | Required by the brief and by us. |
| Workflow | Private GitHub repo, one issue per task, a branch and git worktree per issue, parallel agents each in their own worktree, pull requests merged with merge commits | Commit straight to main | Keeps history and lets agents work in parallel without stepping on each other. |
| Agent log | `SessionEnd` hook exports every session (and subagent) transcript to `docs/agent-log/<session-id>.md` and commits it; home directory path redacted | Manual export | Required by the brief, zero effort once set up. |

## 2026-10-22 — Year range and data policy (from the data survey, issue #1)

Full findings in `docs/data/QUALITY.md`; sources per file in `data/raw/<carrier>/SOURCES.md`.

- **Years: 2023 through 2026**, under each year's January list prices
  (USPS 2023 uses the July 2023 tables, when Ground Advantage launched).
  2022 is dropped from the MVP because USPS sold a different product set.
  FedEx 2027 rates are already published and are kept as an optional forward year.
- **Base rates are parsed** from USPS CSV zips, FedEx XLSX (2022, 2025–2027)
  and text PDFs (FedEx 2023–2024, UPS all years), each validated against
  hand-checked prices.
- **Surcharge rules are curated** into a CSV with a source file and page per
  row, rather than parsed from prose PDFs.
- **Fuel surcharge:** per-year default from FedEx's published history,
  applied to UPS as a proxy and flagged; the UI slider overrides it. USPS has none.
- **Announced increases:** FedEx and USPS from primary sources; UPS from
  trade press, marked secondary.
- **Raw files:** only spreadsheets, CSV zips and small HTML snapshots are
  committed (about 8 MB). All PDFs are gitignored and restored by
  `data/fetch_raw.py` from `data/raw/manifest.csv` (URL, SHA-256, size),
  fetched one at a time with a pause between requests.
- **Citations:** every curated row carries file, page and verbatim quote,
  and a test checks the quote against the document.
- **USPS dimensional weight** verified in the DMM: divisor 166, then 139 from
  2026-07-12, above 1,728 cubic inches, all zones.
- **Schema** for all processed tables and the parcel CSV is fixed in
  `docs/data/SCHEMA.md` before any parser is written.
